title: Why the Novel Took Off
objective: After this level you can explain why the novel boomed in 18th-century Britain, from Robinson Crusoe onward.
summary: Robinson Crusoe (1719) posed as a castaway's own true story in plain, concrete detail. A wider middle-class readership, many of them women, and lending libraries made novels boom.

cards.headline: The word novel comes from a word for "new".
cards.body: It's a shortened form of the Italian novella, from Latin novus, "new". In 18th-century Britain, a new kind of book took off, led by a castaway whose story claimed to be "Written by Himself". Why then, and why there?

cards.headline: A castaway's memoir, invented
cards.body: Daniel Defoe was 59 when he published his first novel, Robinson Crusoe, in 1719. Its title page presented the story as "Written by Himself", as if Crusoe were a real sailor telling the truth. Defoe's style is plain and matter-of-fact, full of vivid, concrete detail: Crusoe builds a raft to strip the wreck of food, tools and sailcloth, then learns to grow corn, barley and rice. One ordinary man, surviving, in close-up.

cards.headline: More readers than ever
cards.body: Behind the boom stood readers. From about 1650, a flood of reading matter spread education through the middle classes, especially to women, and that wider readership shows in the rich growth of the prose novel in the 18th century. In England above all, circulating and subscription libraries lent books to members and shaped popular taste, especially in fiction. You no longer had to buy a novel to read one.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the recipe: new readers, lending libraries, and stories about ordinary lives.

cards.headline: A sensation in letters
cards.body: Then came the hits. Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740), told in letters, follows a servant woman who resists her employer and is rewarded with marriage. It was a publishing sensation, selling in large numbers and provoking parodies, among them Henry Fielding's Shamela (1741). When people start writing parodies of your book, you know it has arrived.

questions.prompt: Don Quixote (Level 56) mocked romances full of knights and giants. What did Robinson Crusoe offer readers instead?

options.label: A knight who defeats real giants
One ordinary man's survival, told in plain, concrete detail
A poem about gods and heroes
Love letters between a servant and her employer

questions.explanation: Instead of knights and giants, Defoe gave readers a raft, tools and a barley crop: an ordinary man's survival in close-up.
